title: Navigation for a developer-tool company
excerpt: The header should map jobs engineers already have: docs, price, changelog, and a way to try the product. Department names send them to the repository instead.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass. The article is about labels that say what is actually open, in words people already use.
caption: A label should say what is inside, as plainly as a sign in the glass. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a developer-tool header include?
faqs.answer: Include docs, a way to try the product, pricing, and the changelog, in those kinds of words. Add source or about if they are real jobs. Leave the blog, careers, and monthly campaigns out of the first row.

faqs.question: What should the try link open?
faqs.answer: It should open the mechanism: a sandbox, a copyable install, or a signup that creates a project. If it opens a sales form, the label is wrong or the destination is wrong. Use one verb for that path across the site.

faqs.question: How do you test navigation labels?
faqs.answer: Ask an engineer who does not know the sitemap to find the install, the price, the changelog, and who maintains the tool. The first place they click is what the label means. Also reach the try path from a keyboard, with a visible focus state.

sources.title: Influencing title links in search results

markdown:
A developer-tool company website navigation is a map of jobs, not a list of departments. An engineer who is skeptical of marketing should see words they already use, and one path that tries the product. Docs. Pricing. Changelog. Try. If the header says platform, solutions, and resources, they will assume the product is a brochure and open the repository instead, if you even linked it.

Keep the map short. This reader has a low tolerance for menus that exist to house content marketing. A link earns a place when it helps them run the tool, judge the cost, see what changed, or confirm who maintains it. Everything else can live one step down, or not at all.

## Jobs they already have

The jobs are practical. Read the docs. Try the tool. See the price. Read the changelog. File an issue or open the source, if the source is public. Log in, if there is an account. Book a conversation only when the conversation is a real job, such as a security review, and label it with that job.

Rename anything that sounds like a department. "Product" is weaker than "Docs" when the docs are how the product is understood. "Company" is weaker than a single "About" if you need it. "Resources" is a drawer where proof and blog posts go to be forgotten. If a proof page matters, label it with the constraint it covers, or call it "Proof" and let the page be specific.

Google's guidance on title links asks for titles that say what the page is, clearly enough that a person can choose it in a list. Navigation is that list, written by you. The header label and the document title should match. If the nav says "Changelog" and the title is "What's new at our innovating platform," the map has started to market. Fix the title. Engineers share deep links. The title is what they paste.

A dropdown is justified when two destinations serve one job. Docs and a quickstart, if both are real and different. A dropdown of industries is a different company's menu. Collapse it. One tool, one primary job, one set of labels.

## Words from the tool, not from a campaign

Use the nouns from the product and the docs. If they say "rules," do not say "intelligence." If they say "workspace," define it once in the docs and use it in the nav only if the page is about that object. Labels should finish the sentence "I need to…" without a translator. I need to try it. I need the install. I need the price. I need what broke in the last release.

Pick one verb for the trial and use it in the header, the homepage, and the pricing page. "Install," "Open sandbox," or "Try." Three verbs for one sandbox reads like three products. If a demo for procurement is a second path, label it "Security review" or "Talk to us about a contract," not as a second "Get started." The difference should be obvious in the words.

GitHub or the public issue tracker can be a header item when it is truly the front door for this audience. Do not style it as a lesser cousin of a campaign link. For many tools it is more honest than the blog. Put it where a skeptical reader expects it, in the bar, with the name they know.

Login stays quiet. It is for people who already have an account. The trial is for people who do not. Give the trial the emphasis. Give login the word "Log in," spelled as a verb, not a cute metaphor.

## One path that tries the product

The try item should be present on every page and should land on the mechanism. A sandbox. A docs page that opens with a copyable command. A signup that creates a project without a meeting. If the item lands on a form called "contact sales," the navigation lied. Change the label or change the destination. Do not keep both lies because the button color tested well.

State the destination's promise in the first line of that page, so the header and the landing agree. "This sandbox runs the sample migration in the browser." The engineer should never wonder whether the click was a newsletter. Agreement between label and page is the whole craft of a small nav.

Do not hide the try path inside docs only. Docs are a job. The trial is a job. Some readers want the long form. Some want the button. Offer both, with labels that do not overlap. A docs page can still contain the command. The header should not force every visitor through a tutorial menu to find it.

On the phone, the try action should be visible without opening a puzzle. A word mark and a button. The rest can sit in the menu. If the menu is where the trial goes to hide, the bar is backwards. This buyer will not hunt. They will bounce to a README hosted somewhere else, and your site will have lost to your own repository.

## What does not belong in the bar

Leave the blog out of the top row unless a specific post is the product, which is rare. Writing can be found from the footer, or from the docs when an article is actually a guide. A header slot spent on "Blog" is a slot not spent on the changelog, and the changelog is the document they use to decide whether you are careful.

Leave careers, press, and the partner form out of the first map. They matter to other people. The footer can carry them without asking every engineer to step around a recruiting campaign.

Leave a search field off until the docs are large enough to need it. On a short site, search admits the labels failed. Fix the labels. When docs are long, search belongs with the docs, not as a way to find the price that should have been a visible word.

Leave campaign links that change every month. A stable bar is a promise that the company knows what it is. A bar that swaps "Launch week" for "Webinar" for "Empowering developers" trains the reader to ignore it. Put launches in the changelog. Let the nav stay boring. Boring is a compliment here.

Count the items. Docs, pricing, changelog, try, and one of about, proof, or source. That is a full bar. If you need more, you probably need a tighter strategy, not a denser header.

## The phone menu and the keyboard

Write the phone list before the desktop hover states. Order it as a sequence. Docs. Try. Pricing. Changelog. Source. About. The try path should be on the screen when the menu opens, or already visible beside the menu button. A long scroll of company links is how the org chart returns.

Do not rely on hover. A menu that opens only under a pointer fails on a phone and fails for anyone using a keyboard. The W3C WCAG overview expects interfaces to be operable, not only visible to a mouse. Click or tap opens the list. Escape closes it. Focus is visible. The try control is a real link or button with a name, not a div that looks like one.

Check the docs nav as part of this work. A marketing header can be perfect while the docs sidebar is a junk drawer. The sidebar is navigation too. Group it by jobs. Install. Configure. Limits. Migrate. A sidebar organized by your internal squads will feel like the department menu you just removed from the homepage.

Read every label next to the page title. Disagreement is a bug. Treat it as one. You would not ship an API whose name and behavior diverged. The site is a smaller interface with the same standard.

## Test the map on a skeptical reader

Ask an engineer who does not know your sitemap to do five tasks. Find how to run it. Find the price. Find what changed recently. Find who maintains it. Find a proof of a hard decision, if you have one. Watch the first place they click. That place is what your label means, regardless of what you intended.

If they go to GitHub for the price, the price is not in the map they trust. Move it. If they search the page with the browser find command for "docs," your word is wrong or your contrast is too quiet. Fix the word before you add a tooltip. A header that needs a tooltip is unfinished.

Then tab through the bar on a laptop. Confirm you can reach the try path without a pointer. Confirm the focused item is obvious. A beautiful bar that traps focus is a bar that fails a portion of the people you claim to serve. This audience notices, and they write about it.

The labels promise an artifact. The pictures have to keep the promise. A header that says docs and a hero that says "empowering developers" over a stock photo is two companies. Read [how to photograph the real screen of the tool](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-developer-tool-company) before you fill the page with a mood the menu did not name.

When you want the bar judged against the jobs an engineer actually has, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the current labels. The work is deciding which ones deserve the first row.
